Neonatal goats, or kids, typically emerge with a wet weight at birth of 2250 grams [Wwb = 2250 grams], a value that reflects the substantial maternal investment characteristic of this medium-sized ungulate. In the first hours following parturition, the altricial neonate must quickly achieve a sternal posture and locate the teat, a critical transition from the intrauterine environment to the demands of terrestrial life. The relatively high birth mass, compared to similarly-sized ruminants, likely provides thermoregulatory advantages during the early postnatal period, particularly in the rugged, often cool mountain habitats where ancestral populations evolved. The newborn kid, a precocial neonate, is soon capable of following its dam, though it remains dependent on milk for the initial months of life. This initial body mass sets the stage for the rapid somatic growth that will characterize the suckling juvenile stage, a period during which the young animal must more than double its weight before facing the challenges of nutritional independence and the eventual transition to a herd-based social structure.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of a healthy domestic goat, which maintains a core body temperature of approximately 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], the gestational period has been documented to last 155 days [tg = 155 days]. This gestation length places the goat within the expected range for a caprine of its body size, aligning well with comparative data from other members of the Caprinae subfamily. The duration of pregnancy is a critical life-history parameter, as it dictates the timing of parturition relative to seasonal resource pulses, a factor of paramount importance for neonatal survival. After this gestation is complete, the dam will then enter a period of intense lactation to support the dependent young. The mother's ability to meet the energetic demands of both milk production and her own maintenance during this suckling stage is a key determinant of offspring growth and ultimate weaning success, a dynamic that has been well-studied in managed herds.

The period of nursing dependency for kids concludes with weaning, which typically occurs at 160 days since birth [tx = 160 days since birth] at a core temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. This transition from a milk-based diet to exclusive foraging on solid foods marks a major nutritional emancipation for the juvenile. The timing of weaning is not fixed but is influenced by both maternal condition and the availability of high-quality forage; in resource-rich environments, the process might be accelerated, whereas in marginal conditions, the dam may extend provisioning. Following nutritional independence, the weaned juvenile enters a prolonged sub-adult phase, during which it must refine its foraging skills and navigate the complexities of the herd's dominance hierarchy. This period is characterized by continued somatic growth and the avoidance of predation, with mortality rates often highest during this vulnerable stage before the young goat has attained full adult body size and behavioral competence.

Sexual maturation proceeds along a sexually dimorphic timeline in the domestic goat. Under standard physiological conditions at 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], females typically attain puberty at 406 days since birth [tp = 406 days since birth], while males require a longer developmental period, reaching puberty at 685 days since birth [tp = 685 days since birth]. This pronounced sex difference in maturation rate is a common pattern among polygynous ungulates, where the larger, competitive males delay reproductive activation until they have achieved the body mass and social standing necessary to compete for access to females. The attainment of puberty in the female triggers the onset of regular estrous cycles, governed by photoperiodic cues. In contrast, the male's later puberty coincides with a period of peak testicular growth and the onset of spermatogenesis, preparing the young buck for his role during the subsequent autumn breeding season when competition for mates is most intense.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult female goats has been recorded at 61,000 grams [Wwi = 61,000 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic body mass for the sex. This adult mass is considerably less than that of males, reflecting the sexual size dimorphism typical of the species. Under captive management conditions, where nutritional constraints are minimized and veterinary care is provided, the maximum recorded lifespan for Goat (Capra hircus) reaches approximately 20.8 years [am = approximately 20.8 years] at a temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. In terms of reproductive output, a healthy doe can annually produce approximately 1.5 kids per pregnancy [N_R_i = approximately 1.5 kids per pregnancy], and given that a single parturition is the standard, the frequency of reproductive events is approximately 1.5 gestations per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 gestations per year]. This annual reproductive rate, combined with the relatively high birth mass and substantial adult female body size, positions the goat as a moderately K-selected species, prioritizing investment per offspring over sheer fecundity when compared to smaller domestic livestock.
